lede: Field notes on famous brand identities: the rebrands that worked, the logo redesigns that got reverted in a week, and what every one of them teaches about brand strategy. Written to be read, not skimmed. Skimming allowed.
note: Every teardown here is commentary on publicly reported brand moves. We were not in those rooms. We just take notes so you do not pay for the same lesson twice.

posts.title: The Gap logo redesign: how to undo a brand identity in six days
posts.dek: In 2010, Gap swapped a twenty-year-old logo for something that looked like a placeholder. The internet said no. Six days later, so did Gap.

p: One October morning in 2010, Gap quietly replaced its famous blue box, the one it had worn for about twenty years, with a plain black wordmark and a small blue gradient square tucked over the P. No campaign. No story. Just a new logo sitting on the website like nothing happened.

The internet noticed within hours. Designers mocked it, customers made parody generators, and the whole thing became a case study in how not to run a logo redesign. Six days later, Gap brought the old logo back and called the episode a lesson in listening.

The new mark was not evil. It was just empty. A brand identity is a container for twenty years of memory, and Gap tipped the memory out without pouring anything back in. There was no brand strategy underneath the change, no positioning shift the design was expressing, no reason a customer could repeat in one sentence.
That is the actual failure. Not the gradient square, although the gradient square did not help. A logo redesign with no strategy behind it is redecoration, and customers can smell redecoration.
First: brand equity is real money. Gap reportedly spent a serious budget on the new identity, then spent the goodwill of every customer who had to watch it happen, and got nothing back for either.
Second: a rebrand needs a reason that survives a hallway conversation. If the answer to 'why did you change it?' is 'it felt dated', you do not have a reason. You have a mood.
Third: if you must retreat, retreat fast. The six-day reversal is the one thing Gap did brilliantly.

Change the logo when the strategy changes, and make the design carry that story. If there is no story, keep the logo and fix what is actually broken. This is exactly why we do branding strategy-first, and why every logo design we ship comes with the reasoning attached.

posts.title: Tropicana's packaging redesign: the carton that drank its own sales
posts.dek: In 2009, Tropicana redesigned its carton so thoroughly that shoppers could no longer find it. Sales reportedly dropped by about a fifth in weeks. The old design came back. The lesson stayed.

p: Tropicana's classic carton had one unforgettable image: an orange with a striped straw stuck in it. Silly, literal, and instantly recognisable from across a supermarket aisle. In 2009 the brand replaced it with a sleek glass of juice, a new typeface, and a minimal layout that whispered where the old one waved.

Shoppers walked straight past it. Reports at the time put the sales drop at roughly twenty percent within weeks, a number worth tens of millions of dollars. Within about two months, the original design was back on shelves.

The new pack was objectively prettier. It was also invisible. Tropicana confused brand identity with decoration and threw away its most valuable visual asset, the thing marketers call a distinctive brand asset and shoppers call 'the one with the straw in the orange'.

Brand recognition does not live in taste. It lives in memory. The straw-in-orange was a memory shortcut built over decades, and the redesign deleted the shortcut while keeping the product identical. Customers did not reject the juice. They simply never saw it.

sections.h: What it teaches about visual identity
p: Audit what people actually recognise before you touch anything. Sometimes the ugliest element on the pack is the entire brand.
Test recognition at a distance, not admiration up close. A design review happens at arm's length; a purchase happens from three metres away, at speed, with a toddler in the trolley.
And write it all down. A proper set of brand guidelines exists precisely so nobody redesigns the one thing that was doing all the work.

Before any redesign, list your distinctive assets and mark the ones that carry recognition. Protect those like revenue, because they are. If you are not sure which parts of your visual identity are load-bearing, that is an audit worth doing before the redesign, not after. It is the first thing we check in every branding project.

posts.title: Twitter to X: the most expensive logo deletion in branding history
posts.dek: In 2023, one of the most recognised brand names on earth was replaced with a letter. Analysts put the value written off in the billions. You cannot buy a clearer lesson in brand equity.

p: In July 2023, Twitter became X. The bird, one of the few logos on the planet that needed no name beside it, was retired overnight. 'Tweet', a verb the brand had somehow pushed into the dictionary, went with it.

Brand analysts estimated the abandoned equity in the billions of dollars. Whatever the exact figure, the shape of it is not in dispute: a globally recognised brand identity, built over seventeen years, was switched off in an evening.

Gap retreated. Tropicana retreated. X did not, because this was not a redesign that misfired. It was a deliberate repositioning: the owner wanted an everything-app called X and was willing to pay the brand equity bill for it.
That makes it the purest demonstration of what a rebrand really is. It is not a new logo. It is a strategic decision with a price tag, and the logo is just the receipt.

sections.h: What it teaches about brand strategy
p: Naming is compounding. Every year a name is used, recognised and repeated, it gets more expensive to replace. That is also the argument for getting the name and the brand positioning right early, while changing them is still cheap.
Verbs are the jackpot. When your brand name becomes the verb for the category, you have won a prize almost no marketing budget can buy. Deleting one is a choice you get to make exactly once.
And repositioning can justify almost anything, if the new position is real. The jury on X is still out. The invoice, however, has already been paid.

Know what your brand equity is worth before you spend it. Most companies have the opposite problem to X: not too much recognition, but too little, which is a cheaper and much more fixable problem. Fixing it is literally our whole job. Start with the brand build, or see what it costs.

posts.title: Airbnb's Bélo: the rebrand the internet mocked, then quietly copied
posts.dek: In 2014, Airbnb launched a symbol the internet turned into a joke within hours. A decade later it is one of the most recognised marks in travel. Both things are lessons.

p: In 2014 Airbnb replaced its bubbly blue wordmark with the Bélo: a looped symbol meant to stand for belonging, drawn simple enough for any host to sketch on a chalkboard. The launch came with a manifesto, a film, and a level of sincerity the internet found irresistible. Mockery arrived on schedule, most of it anatomical.
Airbnb did not blink. No retreat, no apology tour. The symbol stayed, the strategy stayed, and the jokes ran out of fuel in about a week, roughly the time it took Gap to surrender in 2010.

sections.h: Why it worked when others failed
p: The Bélo had what the Gap redesign never did: a real strategy underneath. 'Belong anywhere' was a genuine positioning, the product actually delivered it, and the mark expressed it. When the design connects to something true, early mockery is weather, not climate.

There is also a structural lesson. Airbnb designed the symbol to work without the wordmark, at app-icon size, on a door sticker, embroidered on a pillow. That is logo design done as system design, which is the only way it survives contact with the real world.

sections.h: What it teaches about riding out a rough launch
p: Day-one reactions measure surprise, not quality. The internet reviews change itself, loudly, and then moves on.

Hold your nerve only if the strategy is real. Airbnb could stand firm because the mark meant something. Gap could not, because there was nothing to stand on. Same backlash, opposite endings, and the difference was never the design. It was the brand strategy underneath it.

Build the meaning first, then the mark, then expect a bumpy week and plan for it. If your identity can explain itself in one sentence, it can survive a news cycle. That one sentence is the hardest deliverable in a brand build, and the reason a serious one starts with strategy instead of sketches.

posts.title: Mastercard dropped its own name. The logo did not even flinch
posts.dek: In 2019, Mastercard removed its name from its logo and let two overlapping circles do the talking. It is what winning at brand recognition looks like.

p: After a 2016 refresh of its interlocking red and yellow circles, Mastercard went one step further in 2019 and removed the wordmark entirely from most uses. The company said its research showed the overwhelming majority of people recognised the circles without any text at all.
That put Mastercard in a tiny club with Apple, Nike and Shell: brands whose symbols carry the whole identity, no name required.

Decades of consistency. The circles have overlapped since 1968, surviving every trend cycle that has come and gone since. Mastercard resisted fifty years of redesign temptation, and the reward was a symbol that no longer needs an introduction.

Note what the 2016-2019 work actually was: not reinvention, but reduction. Simplify the shapes, flatten the colours, retire the name. You can only subtract like that when the brand identity underneath is strong enough to hold.

sections.h: What it teaches about brand recognition
p: Recognition is built by repetition, and repetition requires the discipline to stop changing things. The most underrated tool in branding is a strict set of brand guidelines applied for years without exceptions.
Also: a nameless logo is a milestone, not a starting point. Removing your name works after decades of showing up identically. Doing it in year two is not confidence. It is hide and seek.

Design a mark worth repeating, then repeat it until the market can draw it from memory. Consistency is compounding, which is exactly what brand guidelines are for, and why a logo should be drawn to survive decades, not seasons.

posts.title: Jaguar's Copy Nothing rebrand: brave repositioning or expensive dare?
posts.dek: In late 2024, Jaguar launched a rebrand with no cars in it and split the internet in half. Whatever you think of it, it is the most instructive branding argument in years.

p: Jaguar unveiled a new identity in November 2024: a lowercase geometric wordmark, a 'Copy Nothing' manifesto, and a launch film full of colour and fashion, with not a single car in sight. The growler cat was tamed into a minimal mark, and the whole thing pointed at an electric, ultra-premium future.

Half the internet called it brave. The other half called it the end of civilisation, which the internet also says about font changes. The debate itself became the campaign: everyone was suddenly talking about a heritage brand that had spent years being politely ignored.

Strip the noise and the move is textbook repositioning: Jaguar chose to trade its existing audience for one it does not have yet, moving upmarket and electric. The rebrand is the public announcement of that trade.

That is what makes it different from Gap's drift or Tropicana's decoration. Agree or not, there is a strategy here, stated out loud, with the design doing exactly what the strategy asked. The risk is in the bet, not in the craft.
A rebrand can only be judged against its goal. If the goal is a completely new audience, outrage from the old one is not necessarily failure. It might be the plan working.

Attention is a currency, but it has to be converted. Being talked about is step one; being chosen is the score. The Jaguar verdict arrives when the products do, which is a longer game than a launch week.
And heritage is an asset you can spend, like any equity. Just know what you are buying with it, because it does not refill.

If you reposition, commit like Jaguar: say the new position out loud and make every surface agree with it. The rebrands that die are the half-hearted ones, new logo, old promise, confused customer. Deciding the position clearly is the first move of every brand build we run, and the one we refuse to skip.
